Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Eli: I checked the left door and the lower drawer this morning. The door’s slightly out of square, but the hinges are sound. The drawer runners have a little wax buildup; I’m cleaning those before we decide whether the drawer needs any adjustment.

Noor: I’ve photographed the back panel and the inside of both doors. There are pencil marks on the right door, including “ pantry ” in faded graphite. I’ll leave that in place and add a close-up to the condition folder.

Mara: Thanks. The finish is dull in patches, especially near the handles, but I don’t see a reason to strip it. I tested a small area under the top lip with mineral spirits; the cloth picked up grime, and the finish stayed intact.

Theo: I’m sorting the hardware now. There are six brass pulls, but one is a later replacement with a slightly different screw spacing. I’ve put that one in a labeled envelope instead of trying to make the older holes fit it.

Eli: The rear right foot has a split along the grain. It doesn’t move under light hand pressure, and the glue line looks old. I’ll keep checking it while I work on the drawer, rather than clamping it just because it looks rough.

Noor: I found a folded receipt tucked behind the back panel. It’s dated 1958 and lists “one sideboard repair” in blue ink. I scanned both sides, placed it in an archival sleeve, and noted where it was found.

Mara: For today, I’m keeping the work to these steps:
1. Finish the gentle surface cleaning on the top and doors.
2. Check the drawer fit with the runners clean and dry.
3. Record the split foot and the old repair marks before moving the piece.

Theo: The top has two shallow cup rings near the back edge. They’re visible in raking light but hard to see straight on. I’m not sanding them; I’ve taken photos with a scale beside the rings for the condition notes.

Eli: Drawer is back in the case, and it slides more evenly now that the runners are clean. There’s still a little resistance in the last inch. I’m checking whether the rear stop is sitting crooked before I touch the wood.

Noor: I updated the photo names to include the view and date, so the door interiors won’t get mixed up with the outside shots. The receipt scan is in the same folder, but I kept it separate from the furniture images.

Mara: The sideboard’s finish looks warmer after the dry dusting, though the lighter patch below the left pull is still there. That might be wear from hands over time. I’ve added it to the notes without trying to blend it in.

Theo: The right door’s lower hinge has a thin fiber washer under one leaf. It’s compressed but still present. I took a close-up before lifting the door, and I’ll keep the washer with that hinge if we need to remove it later.

Eli: The rear stop was a little loose, not crooked. I snugged its existing screw by hand and tried the drawer again; the last inch feels smoother. I didn’t enlarge the hole or add a new screw.

Noor: I also measured the case: 124 centimeters wide, 47 deep, and 86 high, including the top. The dimensions are on the intake sheet now. The piece is on padded blocks while we check the feet and the underside.

Mara: There’s a strip of newer pine along the inside of the left drawer side. The saw marks and pale color make it stand out from the older oak. We’ll keep it documented as a previous repair; I haven’t covered or altered it.

Theo: I used a soft brush around the brass escutcheons, then a dry cotton cloth on the pulls. The darker tarnish is still in the recessed details. I’m leaving that rather than polishing the hardware bright and changing its appearance.

Eli: I checked the underside with a flashlight. There’s a small paper label near the back rail, partly rubbed away, and the remaining print looks like “H. Morris.” I photographed it in place instead of trying to lift the paper.

Noor: The owner called during lunch and asked whether the pencil word inside the door was new. I told her it was visible in the first photos and appears faded. She said, “That was there when I was little,” so I added her comment to the history notes.

Mara: The clean cloths are drying on the rack, and the used ones are bagged separately. I’ve written down the mineral spirits test location so nobody repeats it on another area by accident. The sideboard is still in the same bay.

Theo: I found one loose pin in the small brass latch, but the latch still turns. I placed the pin in a tiny parts cup with the latch label. I haven’t tried to straighten it; it’s easy to lose against the dark bench mat.

Eli: I’m leaving the drawer out overnight so the cleaned runners can air-dry fully. The drawer is supported on the padded table, and I put a note on the case so it’s clear why it isn’t in place. No parts are missing.

Noor: I’ve got the new photos uploaded, including the foot split, the cup rings, the receipt, and the paper label. The owner’s comment is recorded as a quote, and I kept the exact wording from the call in the notes.

Mara: That covers my update. Tomorrow I’ll look at the drawer fit again with the runners dry, then compare today’s photos with the intake images.
